osm-relation-9620215.hook: A fictional castaway and real lighthouse builders share this little tidal island.
osm-relation-9620215.overview: Erraid links the working coast of the lighthouse builders with the imagined coast of Robert Louis Stevenson. In Kidnapped, David Balfour is stranded here without realising that the island is joined to Mull when the sea recedes.

facts.title: In a novel
facts.text: David Balfour spends part of Kidnapped on Erraid after a shipwreck.

facts.title: Lighthouse country
facts.text: Stone for Dubh Artach lighthouse was quarried here; lighthouse keepers also had cottages on the island.

facts.title: A changing shoreline
facts.text: Erraid is a tidal island beside Mull. Its connection to the land is part of the story, rather than a permanent geographical boundary.

timeline.text: The Northern Lighthouse Board cottages date from this period.
Erraid featured in an episode of New Lives in the Wild.

related.reason: Follow another island that became part of a novelist’s working life.
Compare Stevenson’s fictional castaway with Synge’s observations of island life.

staffa.hook: Cooling lava made the columns; a sea cave helped inspire a concert overture.
staffa.overview: Staffa brings geology and music unusually close together. Fingal’s Cave opens into cliffs of basalt columns, and the island’s caves and sea inspired Mendelssohn’s Hebrides overture.

facts.title: Natural columns
facts.text: The columns around Fingal’s Cave are basalt, a volcanic rock.

facts.title: Music from a landscape
facts.text: Mendelssohn’s Hebrides overture is associated with his response to Staffa and its caves.

facts.title: A place once inhabited
facts.text: A family was still living on Staffa when Joseph Banks visited in 1772; the island later became uninhabited.

timeline.text: Joseph Banks visited and helped bring Staffa wider attention.
Staffa was given to the National Trust for Scotland.

related.reason: Compare Staffa’s basalt columns with Eigg’s different volcanic landscape.
Follow the basalt connection across to Northern Ireland.
Compare this island with Anglesey, a much larger Welsh island linked to the mainland by bridges.

iona.hook: A small island became a centre of monastic learning with connections far beyond its shore.
iona.overview: Iona’s influence grew from the community associated with Columba. Its religious history sits within a living island, where the village, landscapes and continuing community matter alongside the abbey.

facts.title: Early monastery
facts.text: Columba established a monastic community on Iona in 563.

facts.title: More than an abbey
facts.text: Baile Mòr is the island’s main settlement; Iona is also an inhabited community.

facts.title: A continuing tradition
facts.text: The modern Iona Community was founded in 1938 as an ecumenical Christian community.

timeline.text: Columba established his community on the island.
The modern Iona Community was founded.

related.reason: Follow the connection between island monasteries and Northumbrian Christianity.
Compare a sea-island monastery with one on Lower Lough Erne.

osm-relation-1663615.hook: A community buyout and a shared renewable electricity grid changed this island’s story.
osm-relation-1663615.overview: Eigg is a useful place to explore how an island community can shape its future. Community ownership and an electricity system combining several renewable sources sit beneath the distinctive volcanic ridge of An Sgùrr.

facts.title: Community ownership
facts.text: The Isle of Eigg Heritage Trust bought the island in 1997.

facts.title: Shared electricity
facts.text: Eigg’s electricity system combines hydro, wind and solar generation, with backup provision.

facts.title: A volcanic skyline
facts.text: An Sgùrr is formed from pitchstone, above older volcanic rocks.

timeline.text: The island passed into community ownership.
Eigg’s island-wide electricity system was switched on.

related.reason: Compare two striking landscapes made from volcanic rocks.
Explore a different kind of small island community near Mull.
Compare community renewal with the history of an island community that left.

st-kilda.hook: Stone storage huts preserve the traces of a community that chose to leave in 1930.
st-kilda.overview: Hirta is the main island of the St Kilda group. Its surviving village and stone storage huts help explain how people lived in an Atlantic landscape that is also important for seabirds.

facts.title: One island in a group
facts.text: Hirta is the largest island in the St Kilda archipelago.

facts.title: Food and storage
facts.text: The distinctive stone huts called cleitean were used for storage.

facts.title: Human and natural heritage
facts.text: St Kilda’s World Heritage recognition covers both its natural and cultural significance.

timeline.text: The remaining 36 islanders left Hirta at their own request.
St Kilda was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List; its recognition was later extended.

related.reason: Compare the departure of one island community with the renewal of another.
Explore another island with traces of a former resident community.
Follow a different island’s conservation story in Manx waters.

lundy.hook: An island’s puffin coins became the subject of a court case.
lundy.overview: Lundy’s story includes much more than its position in the Bristol Channel. Its local coins, lighthouse history and conservation work show how a small island can develop a distinctive identity while remaining closely connected to the mainland.

facts.title: Puffin money
facts.text: Half Puffin and One Puffin coins were issued in 1929; their issue led to a prosecution under the Coinage Act.

facts.title: Granite landscape
facts.text: Much of Lundy is granite, with steep coastal cliffs.

facts.title: Conservation and care
facts.text: The island was given to the National Trust in 1969 and is managed by the Landmark Trust.

timeline.text: The Puffin coins were issued.
An appeal against the coinage conviction was dismissed.
The island was given to the National Trust.

related.reason: Compare two islands cared for by the National Trust.

lindisfarne.hook: A tidal island connects the stories of monks, manuscripts and a Viking raid.
lindisfarne.overview: Holy Island’s history links Northumberland to the wider world of early medieval Christianity. Its monastic community and later castle occupy an island whose physical connection to the coast is repeatedly covered by the sea.

facts.title: Changing connection
facts.text: Holy Island is tidal; the road connection is not a permanently dry link.

facts.title: Monastic history
facts.text: Aidan founded a monastery here in 635, building links with the Christian community of Iona.

facts.title: Layers of history
facts.text: The priory ruins and the much later Lindisfarne Castle belong to different chapters of the island’s history.

timeline.text: Aidan founded the monastery.
A Viking raid on the monastery was recorded.

related.reason: Return to the island community associated with Aidan’s mission.
Compare this monastic landscape with a lake-island monastery.

eel-pie-island.hook: A Thames island hotel became a stage for British jazz, blues and rock.
eel-pie-island.overview: Eel Pie Island shows how an island can be culturally significant in the middle of a city. Its hotel’s music history sits alongside boatyards, artists’ studios and an island community connected to Twickenham by a footbridge.

facts.title: An island in a river
facts.text: Eel Pie Island is in the Thames at Twickenham.

facts.title: Music history
facts.text: The Rolling Stones and the Who were among the acts that played at the island hotel.

facts.title: A working island
facts.text: Boatyards and artists’ studios form part of the island’s more recent story; private plots are not public attractions.

timeline.text: The island’s first bridge was built.
The former Eel Pie Island Hotel burned down.

related.reason: Follow another island with an influential creative history.
Compare a musical island’s influence with a literary island’s.

brownsea.hook: An experimental camp on this harbour island helped launch the Scout movement.
brownsea.overview: Brownsea combines conservation, industry and social history within Poole Harbour. The remains of its pottery venture and the memory of the 1907 camp add different layers to a landscape now associated with woodland and wildlife.

facts.title: A movement begins
facts.text: Baden-Powell held an experimental camp for boys here in 1907.

facts.title: An industrial chapter
facts.text: A nineteenth-century pottery used the island’s clay; the venture closed in 1887.

facts.title: Conservation
facts.text: The National Trust and Dorset Wildlife Trust have both played roles in protecting the island.

timeline.text: The experimental camp took place.
The National Trust agreed to buy Brownsea.
Brownsea opened to the public under the National Trust.

related.reason: Compare another National Trust island with a very different landscape.

osm-relation-6045364.hook: A bridge changed the connection to Mayo, but Achill kept a distinctive island identity.
osm-relation-6045364.overview: Achill is a good place to question what makes an island an island. A permanent road link joins it to the mainland, while its communities, Irish-language history and landscape retain a distinct identity.

facts.title: An island with a bridge
facts.text: Achill has been connected to the mainland by a bridge since 1887.

facts.title: Language and place
facts.text: The history of Achill’s Irish includes influences associated with both Connacht and Ulster.

facts.title: A railway nearby
facts.text: Achill railway station was on the mainland, despite its name.

timeline.text: The first bridge across Achill Sound was completed.
Achill railway station opened on the mainland.
The railway station and line closed.

osm-relation-8609288.hook: A cable car crosses the sound between this island and the Beara Peninsula.
osm-relation-8609288.overview: Dursey’s cable car gives the island an unusual relationship with the mainland. Its wider history includes a signal tower, earlier settlement and the challenges of sustaining a very small island community.

facts.title: Across the sound
facts.text: A cable car connects Dursey to the mainland across Dursey Sound.

facts.title: An older communications network
facts.text: A ruined signal tower dates from the Napoleonic Wars.

facts.title: A dated population
facts.text: The 2022 census recorded three permanent residents; that is a census snapshot, not a live count.

timeline.text: The island’s post office closed.
The cable car reopened after refurbishment of its infrastructure.

osm-relation-8158177.hook: Island life helped shape Synge’s writing above a landscape of limestone pavements.
osm-relation-8158177.overview: Inis Meáin, the middle Aran island, connects literature with the physical work of island life. Its limestone surface, stone structures and association with J. M. Synge give several ways into its story.

facts.title: A writer’s stays
facts.text: Synge stayed on the island during visits between 1898 and 1902, drawing inspiration from stories he heard.

facts.title: A limestone landscape
facts.text: The island is geologically related to the Burren, with limestone pavements divided by fissures.

facts.title: Remembering the writer
facts.text: Teach Synge is the restored house associated with the writer’s stays.

timeline.text: Synge made the island visits associated with his writing.
The restored Teach Synge opened to the public.

related.reason: Compare two islands that became part of a writer’s imaginative world.

osm-relation-319479.hook: A round tower and former river-piloting community share this Shannon island.
osm-relation-319479.overview: Inis Cathaigh, also known as Scattery Island, brings together monastic history and the working Shannon Estuary. Its surviving tower and church ruins tell one story; the former river-piloting community tells another.

facts.title: Monastic remains
facts.text: The island has a ruined monastery associated with Senan and a surviving Irish round tower.

facts.title: Working on the Shannon
facts.text: River pilots and their families formed an island community in the nineteenth century.

facts.title: Several kinds of heritage
facts.text: A lighthouse and an artillery battery add later layers to the monastic landscape.

timeline.text: The foundation of Senan’s monastery is traditionally placed in this period.
The island became home to a community of Shannon Estuary pilots and their families.
The island was bought by the state heritage service Dúchas.

osm-relation-6046655.hook: Pilgrimage, farming and a legendary burial tradition meet on Ynys Enlli.
osm-relation-6046655.overview: Ynys Enlli, also known as Bardsey, lies off the Llŷn Peninsula. Its story combines a medieval pilgrimage destination with a farming island and a landscape of unusually mixed ancient rocks.

facts.title: Pilgrimage
facts.text: In medieval tradition, three pilgrimages to Bardsey were considered equivalent to one to Rome.

facts.title: Tradition and evidence
facts.text: The association with 20,000 saints is a religious tradition, not a verified count of burials.

facts.title: Mixed rocks
facts.text: The island’s geology includes the Gwna Mélange, a mixture of rock types and large fragments.

timeline.text: St Mary’s Abbey was dissolved.
The island school closed.

related.reason: Compare two islands with continuing religious significance.

osm-relation-3998376.hook: A lake island’s round tower preserves a long history of monastic learning.
osm-relation-3998376.overview: Devenish is in Lower Lough Erne, rather than at sea. Its monastic remains make it a useful comparison with better-known coastal holy islands: water separated communities, but could also connect them.

facts.title: A lake setting
facts.text: Devenish is an island in Lower Lough Erne, County Fermanagh.

facts.title: A monastic tradition
facts.text: The monastery is traditionally associated with Mo Laisse in the sixth century.

facts.title: A distinctive tower
facts.text: The round tower has four upper windows facing the cardinal directions.

timeline.text: Traditional accounts place the monastic foundation in this period.
The monastic settlement was burned.

rathlin.hook: An early wireless link connects Rathlin’s lighthouse history with the beginnings of radio.
rathlin.overview: Rathlin combines communications history with a striking geological landscape. Basalt sits above older limestone, while the island’s seabirds and lighthouses offer further ways to understand its place off the Antrim coast.

facts.title: Early radio
facts.text: An 1898 wireless link connected Rathlin’s East Lighthouse with Ballycastle.

facts.title: Layers in the landscape
facts.text: Basalt overlies older limestone on Rathlin.

facts.title: Seabird conservation
facts.text: The island is important for seabirds and has an RSPB reserve.

timeline.text: The Annals of Ulster record a Viking raid on the island.
The wireless telegraph link with Ballycastle was established.

isle-of-man.hook: Manx language, Norse connections and self-government meet in the Irish Sea.
isle-of-man.overview: The Isle of Man is a self-governing Crown Dependency with a distinct history. Its Manx language and connections with the Norse world provide a wider context for the smaller islands around it.

facts.title: Distinct status
facts.text: The Isle of Man is a Crown Dependency and is not part of the United Kingdom.

facts.title: A living language
facts.text: Manx is a Gaelic language associated with the island.

facts.title: Motorcycling history
facts.text: The TT motorcycle races began in 1907.

timeline.text: Norwegian sovereignty over Man was ceded to Scotland in the Treaty of Perth.
The lordship revested in the British Crown; the island retained internal self-government.
The first TT races were held.

related.reason: Explore the smaller island immediately off Man’s southwest coast.

guernsey.hook: Victor Hugo wrote major works while living in exile on this Channel Island.
guernsey.overview: Guernsey connects island identity with language, exile and wartime history. Its literary associations sit within a distinct island jurisdiction and a culture with Norman as well as British influences.

facts.title: Literary exile
facts.text: Victor Hugo lived on Guernsey and wrote works including Les Misérables during his exile.

facts.title: An island novel
facts.text: Hugo’s Toilers of the Sea is set on Guernsey and was dedicated to the island.

facts.title: Language
facts.text: Guernésiais is the island’s traditional Norman language.

timeline.text: Victor Hugo arrived on Guernsey.
Toilers of the Sea was published.
Guernsey was liberated from German occupation on 9 May.

osm-way-25987471.hook: A former private island became a bird sanctuary and an observatory.
osm-way-25987471.overview: The Calf of Man is a small neighbour of the Isle of Man across Calf Sound. Its transition towards conservation and its lighthouse history make it a useful companion to the larger island’s story.

facts.title: Conservation history
facts.text: The Calf was donated to the National Trust in 1939 to become a bird sanctuary.

facts.title: Long-term observation
facts.text: The island has had a bird observatory since 1959.

facts.title: Lighthouse history
facts.text: Two Robert Stevenson lighthouses were built on the Calf in 1818.

timeline.text: The island was donated for use as a bird sanctuary.
The bird observatory began.
Ownership transferred to Manx National Heritage.

anglesey.hook: Two nineteenth-century bridges changed the connections of Wales’s largest island.
anglesey.overview: Anglesey, or Ynys Môn, combines a distinct Welsh identity with strong connections across the Menai Strait. Its prehistoric monuments and two famous bridges offer different ways to read a large inhabited island.

facts.title: Welsh identity
facts.text: Ynys Môn is the Welsh name for Anglesey, an island off northwest Wales.

facts.title: Across the strait
facts.text: The Menai Strait separates Anglesey from the Welsh mainland.

facts.title: Two bridges
facts.text: The Menai Suspension Bridge and Britannia Bridge span the strait; the latter was originally a railway bridge.

timeline.text: The Menai Suspension Bridge opened.
The original Britannia Bridge opened.
